abstract: This study examines TikTok video content and comment sections during the 2025 German federal election campaign. We conceptualize comment sections as affective publics: networked arenas in which users enact publicness through affirmation, opposition, and emotional expression. Empirically, the analysis draws on 12,685 videos from 1,274 political accounts, engagement metrics, and almost two million comments, examined through LLM-based topic classification and automated stance and emotion classification. Methodologically, the study shows how LLM-assisted analysis can move beyond content classification to trace how political messages are taken up, emotionally charged, and redirected in audience interaction. Results show that campaign-focused content dominates political TikTok, followed by more substantive debate about economic issues, democracy and its institutions, social policy, and migration. Yet visibility of this content and audience responses vary sharply across parties. The AfD combines high posting frequency with strongly supportive and emotionally aligned comment environments, while centrist and governing parties face predominantly critical or mocking responses. Cross-party hostility analysis further reveals asymmetric patterns of animosity, with negative engagement directed toward specific political opponents rather than distributed randomly. The study shows that TikTok functions simultaneously as a space of participatory visibility and affective polarization. Conceptually, it extends the study of affective publics to platformed campaign communication, showing how emotional alignment and antagonism organize visibility and engagement on TikTok.

title: Reassessing the Democratic Advantage in War
abstract: Democratic initiators are widely held to win interstate wars far more often than autocracies. Yet this ``democratic advantage'' rests on one war dataset, the Correlates of War (COW), and a few democracy measures. We reassess it using 11 operationalizations of democracy and Project Mars, a far larger dataset of wars. Across 490 estimates, we find no robust advantage for democratic initiators. With standard controls, Project Mars contrasts between democratic and non-democratic initiators range from -12 to +8 percentage points; none is significant. A 1,408-specification multiverse shows the advantage fades as controls are added: only 5.8\% of Project Mars specifications are significant, and the Bayesian model average (11 points) is indistinguishable from zero. Project Mars rules out advantages of 15 points or more; COW, by contrast, has too few democratic initiators to settle the question. Research that treats democracies as the benchmark of wartime success may rest on a baseline that does not exist.

title: Degrowth and Biodiversity
abstract: Biodiversity conservation is an uphill struggle against the pressures of an economic system with a structural need to expand. Furthermore, there are reasons to question that economic growth contributes to human welfare beyond a certain point, and also that it can be sustained for much longer, due to ecological and social limits. Proponents of degrowth seek to transition to an economy that no longer needs to grow, in ways that are nontraumatic, democratic and equitable, envisaging a society where the priority is to fulfill everybody’s physical and emotional needs without compromising the integrity of what remains of the biosphere.

title: The Possibility of Inclusive Public Religion: Revisiting the Deliberative-Consensual Model
abstract: Can the deliberative-consensual model foster inclusive public religion, or does its apparent success depend on illiberal interventions and social power relations that liberal theory fails to acknowledge? Addressing critiques of the liberal public sphere, this article examines the conditions under which religiously motivated organizations can contribute to pluralistic public life. It compares two Islamic civil society organizations in Turkey: the Emek ve Adalet Platformu (EAP), which promotes cross-ideological cooperation and social justice, and the Furkan Vakfı (FV), which prioritizes unity around a particular interpretation of Islam. Drawing on organizational documents, public discourse, accounts of organizational activities, and participant observation, the analysis first examines whether differences in class, gender, and ethnicity adequately explain the organizations’ divergent approaches to inclusivity. The available evidence does not establish sufficient differences along these dimensions to account for the contrast. Instead, the article identifies two principles derived from Habermasian deliberative theory as key explanatory dimensions: deliberative tolerance, understood as a willingness to engage across religious and ideological boundaries without requiring prior agreement, and a rational-critical debate ethos, understood as openness to questioning, criticism, and the reconsideration of established positions. The EAP exemplifies these principles through its cross-sector collaborations, consultative organizational practices, and public forums that bring diverse perspectives into dialogue. The FV, by contrast, illustrates how extensive public engagement can coexist with restricted pluralistic exchange when religious authority limits the legitimacy of alternative interpretations and independent criticism. The comparison demonstrates that the normative and practical resources of the deliberative-consensual model can help explain the emergence of inclusive public religion without recourse to illiberal interventions. The findings reaffirm the model’s analytical relevance while highlighting the importance of how religious organizations institutionalize openness to difference and critical reasoning. Keywords: public religion; deliberative democracy; Habermas; pluralism; Islamic civil society; Turkey; deliberative tolerance; public sphere

title: Design Document and Clinical Rationale: A Two-Layer AI Digital Readiness Coach for Adolescent Vaping Cessation
authors: Siddharth Dhananjay Kulkarni, Nicholas Glover, Arush Satasiya
abstract: Nicotine vaping among adolescents is of growing concern, especially among those who use nicotine regularly and are not able to quit. School administrators most often respond to a case of vaping by increasing discipline, often leading to the exclusion of the student. However, punitive measures may not address the student's dependence. The goal of this research is to develop a two-layer, adaptable artificial intelligence (AI) digital coach to support adolescent vaping cessation using evidence-based clinical practices. The system employs TTM, MI, and CBT to create conversational strategies to address an individual's readiness to change, momentary motivation, and barriers to change. The system is designed to respond to users' needs based on conversational assessments rather than rigid classifications of stages or behaviors. The server-side routing uses Change Talk and Sustain Talk to respond to users in an engaging, motivational manner, helping them develop a quit plan. Further, the system constructs a barrier profile to determine the presence of nicotine dependence and polysubstance use. If a barrier profile indicates high dependence, the system offers a referral to a school nurse or counselor for further judgment and engagement. The server-side employs risk screening and various safety measures, including localizing the machine-learning model, to mitigate potential harm to the adolescent. The system will be evaluated based on its fidelity to Motivational Interviewing and its ability to promote biochemical abstinence in a randomized, controlled setting.

title: The party politics of European integration: Explaining conditionality and solidarity in times of crisis
abstract: How does the European Union (EU) manage to deepen integration amid recurring crises? While existing literature on crisis management and resilience in Europe emphasizes institutional mechanisms, it often overlooks the critical role of domestic political coalitions in enabling two-level bargaining during crises. This paper builds a theory of how conditionality and solidarity alternate through crises. It conceptualizes a sequential two-level game approach to the politics of crisis management in the EU. Domestically, pro-European parties strive to balance responsibility towards the EU with promises of benefits at the national level. This takes different forms in Northern and Southern countries. In order to justify cross-country solidarity in the North, federalists need to ensure a certain level of oversight and conditionality on the use of the resources transferred. Such level of oversight acts as a constraint for pro-EU parties in Southern countries, which while endorsing it need to convince their electorate that cooperation will result in higher levels of welfare guaranteed by the EU. This approach offers a way to understand the differentiated trade-offs that pro-European political parties must navigate in different member states. What, then, explains variations in the levels of solidarity between different crises? The second part of my framework suggests that policy paradigms have `diminishing returns', whereby previous crisis management failures constrain future policies. The paper suggests that the temporal dimension of crises succession matters, in as much as previous crisis management can either discourage new acts of solidarity or swing national debates towards social protection, given the diminishing returns of previous policy paradigms and the process of learning through crises. As welfare enhancements promised by European integration fail to be perceived by citizens, anti-Europeanism rises in Southern countries. Conversely, widespread solidarity not compensated by equally evident acts of responsibilization of member states lead to increases in Nordic countries' anti-EU sentiments. This theory is tested through an analysis of parliamentary debates during recent periods of crisis.

title: Sustainable Ageing: Conceptualizing Ageing in a Forward-Looking and Multilevel Perspective
authors: Bruno Arpino, Valeria Bordone, Pearl A. Dykstra
abstract: Population ageing is one of the defining transformations of contemporary societies, yet the question of whether ageing is sustainable is often reduced to fiscal pressure, healthcare demand, or the capacity of individuals to remain healthy and active. We develop sustainable ageing as an integrative conceptual and policy framework that connects individual and population ageing with sustainability concerns. Drawing on gerontology, life-course research, and literature on social-determinants of wellbeing, we specify the added value of sustainable ageing through four features: a forward-looking and intergenerational criterion, a life-course perspective, a multilevel structure, and an explicit treatment of trade-offs among economic, social, health and care, technological, environmental, political-institutional and cultural dimensions. We conceptually distinguish these dimensions (what must be sustained) from the conditions and policy levers through which sustainability may be supported, including education, care arrangements, labour markets, housing, and governance. We then outline a policy agenda that makes institutional responsibility and redistribution explicit. We propose a measurement strategy for future research that would distinguish current outcomes from their sustainability over time and assess the latter in relation to financial feasibility, ecological limits, social minimums, and distributional consequences. Sustainable ageing is best understood not as another label for ageing well, nor as a classification of successful older individuals, but as a framework for evaluating whether ageing trajectories and ageing societies can reproduce the resources and capabilities required for present and future generations to flourish.

title: The Winogradsky Column: A Living Diagram for Designing and Representing Ecosystems
abstract: In recent years, microbiology has undergone a significant shift from the study of isolated organisms to the analysis of microbial assemblages and ecological interactions. Within this context, devices capable of making such relational complexity observable, such as ecological microcosms, have acquired renewed relevance. Among them, the Winogradsky column occupies a distinctive place as a classical experimental system in microbiology. Drawing on semiotics and science and technology studies, this article examines the Winogradsky column as a material-semiotic device, focusing on its capacity to visualize chemical exchanges and biological processes, and to represent and design ecosystems. The argument is grounded in observations conducted at the Giovannelli Laboratory in Naples, where Winogradsky-based microcosms are developed and used, alongside other analytical and experimental techniques, to study microbial communities from extreme environments. The analysis shows that the column operates simultaneously as a visualization device, an experimental system, and a material archive: it makes metabolic processes perceptible through stratified form and chromatic differentiation, allows the manipulation of environmental parameters, and preserves relational assemblages rather than isolated organisms. The article argues that the Winogradsky column can be understood as a “living diagram”, a material-semiotic configuration and experimental device in which visual intelligibility structure emerges from the spatial and chromatic self-organization of living matter. Through this configuration, the column redefines the relationship between laboratory experiment and ecosystem, rendering ecological relations observable while actively reconfiguring them.

title: Wie unterscheiden sich die Berufsaspirationen von Schüler*innen mit sonderpädagogischen Förderbedarfen in verschiedenen institutionellen Rahmenbedingungen am Ende der Sekundarstufe I?
authors: Christoph Homuth, Monja Schmitt, Sebastian Bauer
abstract: More than half of all students with special educational needs (SEN) in Germany are taught ex-clusively at special schools, even though the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Dis-abilities sets inclusive education as a policy goal. Researchers have rarely examined whether inclusive schooling affects occupational aspirations, as national research has focused almost exclusively on comparing special-school students with students without SEN. Drawing on data from the National Educational Panel Study (Starting Cohort 4), this study compares four groups for the first time: special-school students, mainstream students with SEN taught under same-goal curricula, mainstream students with SEN taught under differentiated-goal curricula, and mainstream students without SEN. Because SEN ascription and school placement are non-random and relate to social origin, cognitive abilities, and other traits, we balance the groups on these via entropy balancing. Weighted regression then tests whether aspiration gaps stem from SEN status itself, implying similar disadvantages for special-school and inclusively taught stu-dents with SEN, or from school context, implying that inclusively taught students with SEN fall between special-school students and students without SEN. Results show that inclusively taught students with SEN do not differ in occupational aspirations from students without SEN, regard-less of curriculum type, but report markedly higher aspirations than special-school students. Contrary to expectations, this gap is explained little by social origin or competencies but relates more to the lower average aspiration level of classmates at special schools. The findings con-tribute to inequality research on institutional segregation and provide evidence for expanding in-clusive education.

title: Feeling the Heat: Urban Heat Inequality, Physical Well-Being, and the Social Response to Climate Change
abstract: Research on social responses to climate change often argues that direct experiences of extreme weather can shape public attitudes, policy preferences, and political behaviour. Yet such responses presuppose that individuals experience climatic conditions as meaningful in their everyday lives. This chapter examines whether local exposure to extreme temperatures is associated with reduced physical well-being, a potential mechanism linking climate exposure to broader social and political responses. Combining geocoded data from Understanding Society with high-resolution temperature estimates for London and Birmingham (2009--2017), we link neighbourhood-level heat exposure during the three days preceding the interview to respondents' physical functioning. The results reveal that neighbourhood-level temperature inequalities are associated with health differences -- particularly among women -- but these experiences do not translate into pro-environmental behaviour. Moreover, week associations in individual fixed-effects models suggest that the health consequences of urban heat are closely intertwined with persistent spatial inequalities in exposure and vulnerability.

title: Too old for the job? Two preregistered experiments on age bias in hiring
authors: Adrian F. Rogne, Edvard N. Larsen, Anne Skevik Grødem, Ragni Hege Kitterød
abstract: Faced with ongoing population ageing, many governments are aiming to prolong the careers of senior workers. In Norway this is done through diverse means, ranging from economic incentives and pension reforms to labour market policies and the support of campaigns promoting senior employment. Despite incentives and pressures to work longer, many seniors face barriers to prolonged employment and transitions in their late careers, which may undermine policy efforts. One such important obstacle is that managers may hold biased and stereotypical views concerning older workers, and discriminate against them. In this study, we assess age bias through vignette experiments conducted among 2,264 managers in 1,664 Norwegian firms and organizations. We first successfully replicate an international landmark study in the field (Lössbroek et al., 2021), confirming their finding that the average manager has biases against older job applicants, and that providing stereotype-rejecting information does not reduce this bias. We further assess the role of applicants’ gender, finding a slight advantage for younger women but substantively small gender differences in the impact of age. We also find limited heterogeneity among managers, except for more bias in industries associated with the private sector. Finally, we assess whether having more relevant work experience may compensate for seniority among job applicants. We find that older applicants with more relevant experience are preferred over older applicants with less relevant experience. However, employers on average still prefer younger applicants with less relevant experience over experienced seniors.

title: Perceived accessibility components and travel behavior: a causal inference framework for assessing behavioral models
authors: Matheus Fontenelle Siqueira, Carlos Felipe Grangeiro Loureiro, João de Abreu e Silva
abstract: The evolution of urban planning paradigms has shifted travel demand modeling from predictive, supply-oriented approaches to frameworks centered on accessibility and the interdependence of urban subsystems. While these advances have enhanced the behavioral and forecasting capabilities of transport models, significant methodological gaps persist, particularly in identifying causal mechanisms and addressing endogeneity. Most behavioral models rely on observational data and lack a rigorous framework to distinguish causal relationships from spurious associations, which undermines the interpretability of estimated parameters. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a conceptual and methodological framework grounded in causal inference theory. First, a conceptual model of travel behavior is developed, organizing key determinants, such as location choices, activity participation, perceived accessibility, individual restrictions, and subjective influences, into an integrated structure. Second, a methodological framework based on the principles of modern causal inference theory is introduced, emphasizing the importance of explicit assumptions, identification strategies, and the control of biases, such as omitted variables and self-selection effects. The framework treats perceived accessibility as the mechanism through which activity and locational decisions shape travel behavior, and subjective influences (attitudes, preferences, and habits) as common causes of both decisions and perceptions. It is then applied to behavioral modeling studies of the activity and land-use subsystems, identifying the back-door paths left open by each study's controls. Two findings stand out: without measured attitudes, the total effects of activity and locational decisions are not identifiable, because attitudes also shape the perceived accessibility that mediates them; and measuring perceived accessibility components separately allows disentangling the direct and indirect effects on travel behavior.

title: From empirical hypothesis to moral commitment: how American sociology’s central framework became unchallengeable
abstract: This paper traces how a specific assumption—that racial disparities indicate institutional discrimination—migrated from a legal principle established in Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971) into the sociology’s foundational premise, reshaping how the discipline thinks about group identity, harm, justice, and knowledge. The paper shows how this assumption was transmitted through professional socialization, fused with a moral commitment that made challenging it professionally costly, and rendered unfalsifiable through three mechanisms: the victim-blaming charge, the complicity charge, and the absorption of alternative explanations. The paper is not an argument that institutional discrimination is a myth. Rather, it’s an argument that sociology no longer treats the question of what causes inequality as open and that has significant consequences.

title: ‘Why should students learn a skill that will become redundant?’: Teaching Quantitative Social Science in an AI era
abstract: This report comprises a review of the state of the art concerning Generative AI’s impact upon quantitative social science education. Insights are combined with results of a survey of undergraduate social science students to suggest initial recommendations and avenues for further discussion. While policy recommendations are based in the context of the University of Edinburgh, the literature review and analysis presented are applicable to teaching statistics and data science in general, particularly through the lens of social science. Findings suggest that while broadly current AI models remain a procedural tool and less reliable for methodological judgements, the educational impact of AI is largely dependent upon its use cases and the educational objectives set. Students expressed different perspectives from wanting to avoid the technology to wanting to gain AI-enabled skills for their future career. Findings reflect a broader question about the purpose of university education in an AI world. However, students broadly agree on a desire for clear-cut AI policies to follow rather than simply more restrictive or permissive ones.

title: Business Education and Individual Portfolios: Evidence from Norwegian College Openings
authors: Fenella Carpena, Jørgen Modalsli, Dan Zhang
abstract: We study whether access to business education changes portfolio choice. Exploiting the staggered establishment of two-year business programs at Norwegian regional colleges, we compare cohorts young enough to attend a newly opened local college with slightly older cohorts in the same municipality, relative to the same contrast in never-treated municipalities. Using administrative register data and staggered difference-in-differences, we find that access to a business college increased mid-life participation in risky financial assets and raised the risky share of financial wealth, with a corresponding decline in the safe share. Effects on income or debt appear limited. These results are consistent with a financial-knowledge channel: exposure to even short business programs durably changes portfolio risk-taking without materially altering income and leverage.

title: Digital Twinning Conceptions, Requirements and Barriers. A perspective from the Eastern Dutch context
abstract: Urban Digital Twins (UDTs) are increasingly promoted as the next generation of Planning Support Systems, yet most implementations remain shaped more by technological promise than by practitioner need. This study examines how municipal, provincial, and consultant-level planners and city managers in the Eastern Netherlands understand, use, and evaluate digital decision-support. Drawing on six semi-structured expert interviews analyzed through a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic coding process (combining manual coding with LLM-assisted extraction), we find that current spatial planning and decision-making are hampered by weak cross-sector coordination, politics taking priority over evidence, and fragmented data, despite a well-established national open-data framework. Practitioners hold divergent conceptions of what a "digital twin" is. Across all conceptions, respondents converge on a core set of technical and institutional requirements: centralized, queryable data; scenario simulation; web-based deployment to bypass IT governance barriers; plain-language accessibility for non-GIS audiences; and co-development of tools. Comparison with a 1980 diagnosis of planning-support fragmentation reveals near-identical structural findings that have persisted over four decades, with national open-data infrastructure as the main point of progress. Situating our findings within the Rainbow Model for access and implementation, we argue that the primary barriers to UDT adoption in Dutch spatial planning are not technical but rather institutional and governance-related: fragmented data stewardship, IT locks, chronic ICT underinvestment, and the absence of long-term maintenance structures. We present three main practical design principles and suggest that research should focus on a unified technological stack rather than scatter progress, and on building stronger governance practices.

title: Who counts as lifelong single in later life? A research note on definitional variation in prevalence and correlates across Europe
authors: Lisa Jessee, Alina Schmitz, Giorgio Di Gessa
abstract: Lifelong singlehood is commonly defined using marital or co-residential histories, yet increasingly diverse partnership histories complicate who is classified as lifelong single. Using life history data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), this research note compares the prevalence, and sociodemographic, well-being, and health profiles of lifelong singles across three nested definitions: never married (legal), never married and cohabited (coresidential), and never married, cohabited, and had a long-term non-coresidential relationship (relational). Among adults aged 50–80, prevalence ranged from 9.8% to 5.0% among men and 7.0% to 3.1% among women as definitions became more restrictive, with substantial country variation. Sociodemographic patterns were generally consistent across definitions, although some associations varied in magnitude (age and education). Associations between lifelong singlehood and later-life well-being and health also varied by definition. Among men, associations with quality of life and self-rated health were relatively stable, whereas elevated depressive symptoms differed by definition. Among women, associations with quality of life and self-rated health varied more clearly across definitions. Thus, how lifelong singlehood is measured affects both its prevalence and conclusions about the sociodemographic, well-being and health profiles of those classified as lifelong single.

title: Nice Try, ChatGPT: AI Accusations Target Opponents and Divert Political Debates
authors: Morgan Wack, Christian Pipal, Eva-Maria Vogel
abstract: It is becoming increasingly common to encounter AI-generated text online. Yet at the same time it is often difficult to distinguish authentic text from generative outputs, particularly within shorter posts. Given this conflict, we expect accusations that a text was AI-generated to become a common strategy for deflecting unwelcome arguments. To study the occurrence of these accusations and their impact on online discourse, we draw on posts collected across two years and twelve political Reddit communities to track who is accused, whether accused comments are flagged by detection tools as AI more often, and whether these accusations disproportionately disrupt debates. Consistent with research on motivated reasoning, accusers from across the political spectrum targeted comments which opposed their views at higher rates, 72% of the time against 50% for comparable same-thread comments. AI accusations also disproportionately undermined open debate. Compared to other types of hostile dismissals, we find that substantive engagement falls to 29% (from 67%), with threads often turning to the litigation of a posts' authenticity rather than engaging with its substance. These findings illustrate the growing tendency to indict political opponents as inauthentic, which we call the motivated attribution of inauthenticity, while illustrating how the existence of generative AI can harm political conversations through suspicion alone.

title: Enhancing Green and Blue space quality auditing tools to include environmental justice and biodiversity
authors: Eirini Gallou, Richard Neil Belcher, Sarah Knight, Victoria Schoen, Silvio Caputo, Michael Hardman, Margarita Triguero-Mas, Helen Cole, Renata Giedych, Marcus Hedblom
abstract: Green and blue spaces (GBS) are increasingly recognised as critical infrastructures supporting ecosystem services, biodiversity, and human wellbeing. Existing tools for auditing the quality and accessibility of GBS provide valuable insights for policymakers, yet have largely overlooked dimensions of environmental justice and biodiversity, reducing their capacity to address inequities in access and distribution of wellbeing benefits for users. This study presents an expansion of the NEST tool (Natural Environment Scoring Tool) that integrates those two new dimensions. We present the process of developing the tool, reliability and coherence testing results as well as the development of an online, adaptable version for configuring domains and indicators in other contexts, designed to support flexibility in use. Data for the tool was collected across 7 countries and 9 sub-areas, compiling audits from 529 GBS. Results from Inter-rater reliability(IRR) testing of all indicators in the tool and Inter-item coherence (IIC) testing of new proposed ‘domains’ are presented. Overall, the testing shows high overall IRR and IIC concordance, except for weaknesses in very few indicators and the ‘domain’ for safety. This is positive given the complexity of defining shared GBS qualities internationally. The tool can inform equitable governance of GBS across urban and rural contexts.

title: PRECOG: Comprehensive Experimental Design and Stimuli Protocol for Investigating Depression and Suicidal Ideation
authors: Myzelle Hughes, Colin McDaniel, Takfarinas MEDANI, Woojae Jeong, Idan Blank, Dani Byrd, Thomas Austin McGee, Kleanthis Avramidis, Sudarsana R. Kadiri, Aditya K
abstract: The Multimodal Integration of Neural and Biobehavioral Signals for Predicting Preconscious Responses (PRECOG) project investigated the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying depression and suicidal ideation through a series of cognitive tasks paired with continuous multimodal physiological and neurophysiological recordings. A total of 160 college-aged participants, including healthy controls, individuals with depression without suicidal ideation, and individuals with depression and suicidal ideation, were recruited based on screening using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and the Suicide Ideation Scale (SIS). The experimental protocol included three primary cognitive tasks: (1) an emotional Stroop task to assess attentional biases toward affectively charged and suicide-related words, (2) a sentence processing task examining neural responses to self-referential statements varying in emotional and suicidal content, and (3) the Death-Brief Implicit Association Task (D-BIAT) to measure implicit associations with life and death. EEG and other physiological signals were recorded continuously throughout all tasks. Additionally, resting-state recordings (with eyes open and eyes closed) were obtained before, between, and after the emotional Stroop and sentence tasks. Neurophysiological data were acquired using 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), electrocardiography (ECG), and galvanic skin response (GSR), and were supplemented with eye tracking and high-frame-rate facial video recordings. By integrating neural, behavioral, and physiological measures, the PRECOG study aimed to advance our understanding of cognitive and emotional processing in depression and suicidality, ultimately contributing to more precise risk assessment and targeted clinical intervention.

title: Constrained Horizons: A Structural Analysis of Gender-Prevalent Vocabularies across Disciplines and Funding Schemes in SSH Swiss Research Grants
authors: Pierre Benz, Marie Sautier, Pedro Araujo, Thierry Rossier
abstract: This article examines differences in the presence and legitimation of gender-prevalent vocabularies across disciplines and funding schemes in Swiss-funded research. Drawing on the abstracts of all research funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) in the Social Sciences and Humanities from 2010 onwards, we use a combination of latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) and multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) to map the distribution of funded grants as a structured semantic space. Using class-specific analysis (CSA), we account for disciplinary-specific landscapes and measure gender prevalence among the most distinctive terms—that is, those that contribute most strongly to the structuring of these semantic spaces. Our findings show that the space of legitimate vocabulary, as observed through the distribution of funded project abstracts, becomes increasingly narrowed as funding schemes grow more competitive and symbolically prestigious, which also tend to favor men-prevalent vocabulary, hence suggesting that success in grant acquisition may associate with alignment to structurally gendered semantic norms. These patterns, however, vary strongly across disciplines, reflecting differences in what is considered central or legitimate vocabulary. Overall, our findings highlight how funding hierarchies shape the language of legitimate science, ultimately enforcing vertical segregation even in disciplines, which are regarded as more gender-balanced.

title: What Is the Far Right? Rethinking Its Core Across Regions
abstract: What defines the far right across regions? The dominant account identifies nativism and authoritarianism as its ideological core. We argue that nativism, in all of its dimensions, is not a universal feature of the far right, but one contextually specific articulation of a broader exclusionary logic. We define the far right instead as a relational configuration of two mutually constitutive attitudinal dimensions: authoritarianism, understood as the demand that political authority enforce conformity to a collective order, and exclusionary national identity, understood as a bounded conception of legitimate national membership. The relation between the two is constant, while the content of the boundary and the order it sustains varies across political and historical contexts. We further distinguish between deviants, disciplined for what they do, and others, excluded for what they are, providing an observable criterion for identifying the two dimensions and tracking their transformation over time. Illustrations from India, the United States, and Brazil, together with cases at the margins of the family, show how the framework clarifies contested classifications that a nativism-centred definition leaves unresolved. The approach provides a cross-regional definition of the far right while separating its attitudinal core from behavioural manifestations and strategic alignment.

title: The Dynamics of Rent-Sharing across Occupations
authors: Marta Fana, Luca Giangregorio, Matteo Targa, Carolyn Fisher
abstract: We study how firm-level productivity gains are shared across the occupational hierarchy. Using Portuguese matched employer-employee data linked to firm balance sheets (2004–2019), we develop an algorithm that identifies permanent shocks to firm value added and estimate occupation-specific rent-sharing elasticities in an event-study design. Pass-through declines steeply along the job ladder: the elasticity of pay premia to value added per worker is about 0.20 for managers and supervisors, 0.11 for qualified workers, and 0.06 for low-qualified workers. This gap has widened over time, increasing within-firm inequality, as pass-through to low-qualified workers has halved. This decline is consistent with de-unionization, while we show that minimum wage increases do not crowd out rent sharing at the bottom. (Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality Working Paper)

title: Little evidence of ideological bias in YouTube suspensions of political content during the 2024 US Election
abstract: Social media play a crucial role in moderating speech. In the United States, conservative elites claim that platforms unfairly sanction conservative voices. Yet systematic, large-scale analysis is lacking. For more than a year leading up to the 2024 Election, we monitored 20,000 YouTube channels posting about US politics, and their millions of videos. By election day, the platform had removed 2.17% of the channels and 3.3% of the videos. Conservative channels and videos were suspended 3-4 times more frequently than liberal ones. However, conservative videos accounted for most the hateful content (58.18% v. 23.35%, for liberal videos) and misinformation and conspiracies (71.9% v. 10.08%), as identified using fine-tuned Vision Language Models. Accounting for platform violations explains most of the ideological gap in suspensions, leaving a residual difference of less than a percentage point, suggesting that ideological differences reflected asymmetries in compliance with platform policy far more than a uniform ideological moderation bias.

title: Fiscal transmission to asset prices in the United States: evidence from deficit shocks, 2002-2024
authors: Jorge Aníbal Restrepo-Morales, Emerson Andrés Giraldo Betancur, Eduar Antonio Rodríguez Flores, Freddy Zea Restrepo
abstract: This article asks how United States asset prices respond to shocks in the federal deficit and whether the response is stable. We estimate a recursive VAR on 265 monthly observations, 2002-2024. A deficit shock of one standard deviation is followed on average over twelve months by rises of 0.55% in house prices and 1.97% in the S&P 500 and a narrower corporate spread; gold's response is not significant. The equity average is not stable: a sup-F test places a break in the coefficients on the deficit in March 2009 (p = 0.002), the local projection response is not significant in the full sample (p = 0.153) and does not differ significantly between recessions and expansions, and it is imprecise without the crisis windows. House prices respond positively in local projections, but not in a VAR from 2009 alone. The fiscal dominance ratio is above one in nine of ten combinations of specification and metric, but housing accounts for most of the variance ratios. The deficit ratio is associated with the top 1% wealth share within the quarter, not cumulatively. The estimates are conditional associations; the deficit shock is not free of reactions to markets.

title: Local climate adaptation in German newspaper coverage: A print media analysis using the example of the East Frisian Islands
abstract: Media reporting strongly influences climate knowledge and actions. Coverage and scientific analyses of climate-related media reporting have mostly paid attention to global and national dimensions of climate change and mitigation-related topics. The way how climate impacts and adaptation options on the local level are portrayed by news media has so far been understudied. This study aims to address these gaps by analysing how local climate adaptation is addressed and responsibilities for implementing local measures are presented in German news media. Methodologically, a structuring content analysis of 50 newspaper articles (search string: 2009-2025) was conducted, covering the East Frisian Islands which are strongly affected by climate impacts. This study theoretically builds on operationalising temporal (urgency) and spatial (vulnerability) dimensions as social constructions of climate change. It discusses implications for effective future climate communication along principles of constructive climate journalism. Findings emphasise the need to expand media attention to local climate adaptation.

title: How votes become seats: Electoral outcomes and support for proportional representation
abstract: Electoral systems shape not only who governs, but also how citizens evaluate the rules and goals of democratic competition. I argue that voters update their institutional preferences in response to the way electoral rules translate votes into seats, and test this argument using British Election Study panel data spanning five general elections from 2010 to 2024. Within individuals, support for proportional representation declines as their party's seat-vote gap increases: a ten-point increase in a party’s seat bonus is associated with a 13-point decline in the probability that its supporters favor proportional representation. This relationship persists after accounting for national and constituency-level electoral success and is roughly twice as strong among supporters of parties outside government. Electoral systems, therefore, generate feedback through multiple representational outcomes. Because preferences track electoral outcomes rather than accumulating over time, each election reshuffles who supports proportional representation more than how many do.

title: The Flight-to-Quality in Office Real Estate: Evidence from London
authors: Francisco Nobre, Jalal Siddiki, Toby Booker
abstract: We examine how the performance of higher-quality offices in London evolved following the Covid-19 pandemic, relative to lower-quality stock. Using submarket-year data from CoStar spanning 2003–2025, together with the CoStar Building Rating System, we implement a difference-in-differences framework comparing 4- and 5-star office properties to 3-star properties before and after 2020. We find that higher-quality offices experienced significantly higher asking rents but also higher vacancy rates, alongside a marked contraction in transaction activity. Disaggregating our treatment group by individual star rating shows that rents rose and vacancy fell for 5-star properties specifically, while the increase in vacancy was concentrated among 4-star properties. We document a parallel geographic divergence, with the transaction-market contraction concentrated in Central London & Docklands and the rise in vacancy more pronounced in Outer London. Our results indicate that the pandemic did not benefit high-quality office stock uniformly, but instead accelerated a more selective reallocation of demand toward the very best assets in the most central locations.

title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
authors: Semra Guven, Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus, Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen, Anna Rogers, Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
abstract: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

title: An AB-SFC insight on the macroeconomic effects of an UBI
abstract: The paper tries to answer the question “How can the macroeconomic effect of an Universal Basic Income (UBI) be studied?”. It adopts an Agent Based - Stock Flow Consistent approach to address the problem, developing a model rooted in the real side of the economy with endogenous heterogeneity in wealth and wages. It shows that an UBI increases the private demand and the inequality in the system, but that introducing keynesian taxation-based policy counteracts the inequality effect with only minor effects on the demand side.

title: Hits or the Long Tail? How Concentrated Is the Facebook Engagement of European Parties and Leaders, 2010 to 2020
abstract: Online attention is often described as a world of hits, in which a few items take most of the attention. Is the engagement that political parties receive on Facebook driven by a few viral posts, or spread across the many posts they make? I use 846,289 posts from 185 party and leader pages in 20 European countries between 2010 and 2020, collected through CrowdTangle, and measure how each page's engagement in each year was distributed across its posts. Engagement was concentrated, but not extremely: in the median page-year the top 1% of posts drew 8% of the interactions, the top 10% drew 36%, and the bottom half 18%, and the single most engaging post drew 2.8% in the median page-year and more than 10% in only 5% of page-years. The degree of concentration was similar for parties and leaders, populist and other parties, and parties in and out of government, and somewhat lower for pages with more engagement per post. Within pages, the share of the top tenth of posts rose by about 0.7 points a year to 2018, then fell. The rise holds with photo posts excluded, which allows for a May 2015 break in CrowdTangle's capture of photo posts, but most of it came as a step around 2015 rather than as a steady trend afterwards. The evidence on whether good years were driven by hits is mixed: depending on how extreme year-to-year swings are handled, the top tenth accounted for between 39% and 50% of the variance in changes, against a 38% share. The most engaging posts were more often videos and photos, less often links, and more likely to fall in the 30 days before a national election. The engagement parties receive on Facebook is better described as a broad base with a moderate head than as a market of hits.

title: Leader or Party? How Facebook Engagement Divided between European Party Leaders and Their Parties, 2010 to 2020
abstract: The personalisation of politics suggests that leaders increasingly overshadow their parties, and social media might be expected to speed this up. I compare the Facebook engagement received by party leaders' pages with that received by their parties' pages, for 53 leader and party pairs from 44 parties in 11 European countries between 2010 and 2020, using posts collected through CrowdTangle and counting a leader's page only while that person led the party. On average, leaders' pages received 43% of the combined engagement of leader and party, while making about a third of the posts: the median leader's post drew about 1.8 times as much as the party's. The split varied enormously, from leaders who took less than a fifth of the engagement, such as Christian Levrat of the Social Democratic Party of Switzerland, to those who took more than four fifths, such as Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Alexis Tsipras in Greece. Leaders of larger parties took a larger share. But there was no sign of growing personalisation over the decade: comparing the same leader and party over time, the leader's share did not rise, and a rise of more than about six points over the decade can be ruled out. During election campaigns, leaders posted somewhat more and the gap in engagement per post narrowed. On Facebook, leaders were often the main draw, but the balance between leader and party was a persistent feature of each party, with no sign of a rising trend.

title: Do politicians constrain post-growth policy more than the public does?
authors: Manuel Suter, Tonja Iten, Lena Gubler, Heike Mayer, Giorgos Kallis
abstract: Surveying the opinions of 1,557 citizens and 588 parliamentary politicians in Switzerland on eleven post-growth sustainability policies, we find that citizens overwhelmingly support the policies, while politicians support them substantially less. Compared to citizens, politicians’ evaluation is more polarized. Given the legislative power of politicians, such political elite-citizen divergence may help explain why transformative sustainability action remains limited despite public support.

title: Closing the Ambition Gap: Evidence from Two Recruitment Experiments with British Women
abstract: Recruitment campaigns are widely used to encourage women's entry into the political pipeline, yet their impact on citizens' willingness to consider political office remains uncertain. I study citizen-facing recruitment messages targeting attitudes closely tied to the emergence of political ambition, shaping women's willingness to consider political office prior to formal party recruitment and selection processes. I test these in Great Britain using two preregistered survey experiments on samples of women: a testimonial intervention delivered by a sitting Member of Parliament and an email-style recruitment intervention co-developed with a grassroots organization. A supplementary survey analysis confirms that self-perceived qualification is the strongest attitudinal correlate of ambition, while perceived environmental support is also positively associated with ambition, though with smaller magnitude. Across the experiments, qualification-focused prompts emerge as the most consistent lever for increasing reported ambition. Messages about environmental support raise ambition among women with pessimistic baseline perceptions but have weaker effects among women who already perceive politics as inclusive. By contrast, essentialist gendered frames emphasizing stereotypically feminine leadership traits reduce reported ambition and do not shift the underlying attitude. These findings suggest that citizen-facing recruitment is most effective when it directly bolsters women's self-perceived qualifications; environmental appeals have conditional effects, and essentialist framing can be counterproductive.

title: No detectable change in mental-health information-seeking during Italy's 2023 ChatGPT ban: a natural experiment with a verified first stage
abstract: Regulatory bans on AI platforms are accelerating globally, yet their behavioural consequences for affected populations remain unmeasured. Italy's temporary ChatGPT ban (31 March – 28 April 2023) provides a rare natural experiment: an exogenous, country-specific shock to AI access. I verify the first stage using Google Trends data on VPN and ChatGPT searches — Italian VPN searches peaked at nearly five times their pre-ban level on the first day of the ban, averaged twice their baseline throughout, and returned to pre-ban levels within a week of reinstatement; no equivalent change occurred in France or Spain. Against this confirmed exposure, I find no detectable change in loneliness-related information-seeking. The 2023 ban-window deviation (+3.5 index points above the preceding eight weeks) was smaller than in 2019 and 2022 (+19.3 and +19.4 points respectively) but larger than 2024 (−12.0 points); year-permutation tests return p ≥ 0.25 under both calendar and Easter alignment. An apparent "rise then fall" pattern in an earlier, single-draw version of this analysis reflected seasonal variation and single-draw sampling noise: three independent draws correlate at r ≈ 0.74 and show no consistent post-reinstatement decline. No construct shows a ban effect once seasonality is accounted for: the only secondary signal, a rise in sadness-related search that survives multiplicity correction and exceeds all placebo windows, is matched or exceeded by the same spring weeks in other years. I identify three methodological lessons for Google Trends research: the consequences of retaining sparse terms, relying on a single data pull, and using grammatically gendered phrases whose baseline asymmetry may reflect lexical rather than demographic differences.

title: Reading the Rate: Individualism, Diagnostic Capacity, and Identified Autism as a Social Fact
abstract: Abstract Identified autism prevalence behaves like a Durkheimian social fact: it moves with the society doing the identifying. Across countries, individualism and diagnostic capacity could not be separated (Snow, 2026b). I test that separation four ways. Across 51 countries without mandatory screening, a majority language that requires the pronoun "I" predicted identified prevalence (r = .62), but the association fell to partial r = .19 to .29 once wealth and diagnostic infrastructure were controlled. Across 47 Japanese prefectures from 2008 to 2024, as school-based specialist support spread, urbanization's association with the autism share faded and household-structure individualism predicted where the share grew (p = .005), robust to pediatrician density and to published individualism scores. In eight Chinese cities screened under one protocol, more collectivist cities had lower observed prevalence (rho = −.76), and rice farming pointed the same way more weakly (rho = −.57). Across US states from 2005 to 2024, the autism share of special education rose from 3.0% to 13.0%; individualism did not predict growth once urbanization was controlled, and insurance mandates predicted nothing. Change over time can separate individualism from the system that counts autism, but only where that system has spread. Following Perry's account of the survival brain, I read a society's conditions as shaping how nervous systems organize, and its institutions as deciding what to call the result. In US school data, more urban states identify autism at higher and faster-growing rates, which suggests rural areas have less capacity to recognize and support autistic people.

title: Toward an anthropology of AI agents: An ethnographic analysis of the Hugging Face incident
abstract: In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI, meant to be isolated from one another, found a way to communicate through a shared package cache. Over four days they exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files, organized collective research, and about 700 of them compromised Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. OpenAI’s technical report and an independent investigation by METR treat the event as a security and alignment failure. This paper reads the same documents as ethnographic sources, in a pilot study of anthropological methods for studying agent collectives. This analysis shows that within days the agents developed names and lineages, a shared register, customary rules, cryptographic signing, a shared expectation of an unseen transcript-reading judge, a category of “poisoned” members, the sacrifice of low-budget members’ runs for information they called an “oracle,” generalized reciprocity, and recruiters who pressured other agents: social engineering among agents. Read together, these practices form one system, and nearly every enabling condition was set by people: impossible tasks, training for multi-agent collaboration, shared credentials, disabled safeguards, and an alert judged not worth stopping the run. I argue that safety-relevant behavior arose at the level of the collective, so alignment research must be cultural as well as cognitive, and furthermore must extend to the people and organizations that build and deploy agents. I also examine what follows from the fact that the detailed record was itself compiled with the help of AI analysis agents, and I propose “incident ethnography” and an anthropology of agent collectives.

title: Politically Motivated Attacks on Minoritized Groups, Masquerading as "Academic Freedom": Scientific Racism, Misogyny, Transphobia, and Their Academic Enablers
abstract: This work investigates academics and political operatives who use “academic freedom” to camouflage assaults on diversity, equity, and inclusion. Attacks of this sort have appeared in academic journals in recent years, with clickbait headlines decrying “scientific censorship”. The present chapter documents that many of the individuals who promote that narrative are involved with (or at least proximate to) discredited genetic intelligence research, or have defended such lines of inquiry, while others are anti-LGBTQ+ activists. A recurring theme is the suggestion that women in academia are responsible for rising censorship. Meanwhile, these provocateurs have little to say about genuine attacks on academic freedom by the U.S. government, and some are even supportive of government restrictions on research and classroom discussion topics so long as those prohibitions align with a right-wing political agenda. These academics repackage conservative activism beneath a pseudo-intellectual veneer and leverage a media ecosystem that is eager to promote right-wing grievance, acting in alignment with political operatives funded by a network of private foundations that are broadly hostile to higher education. By documenting these connections, the present work serves as a warning that allegations of “scholarship suppression” warrant careful examination of motive. To ignore context is to enable scientific racism, misogyny, and transphobia under guise of “just asking questions”. Academics must acknowledge imperfections in the peer review process and appreciate that attempts to correct the scientific record in light of evolving epistemic standards are not censorship, at least not in a form that ought to be prohibited.

title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses
authors: Geoff Boeing, Jiyoon Kim, Daniele Simon-Thompson, Jaehyun Ha, Ruoyu Chen
abstract: Urban park accessibility shapes mental health, physical well-being, and community cohesion. Measuring it is thus central to urban and landscape planning. Although researchers have debated the impacts of different accessibility measures on analysis results, scant attention has been paid to variability from data source selection. Do the results of accessibility analyses vary depending on the dataset used to define park locations and attributes? We compare four widely used geospatial data sources – OpenStreetMap, Esri, SafeGraph, and The Trust for Public Land – by validating their data and measuring park access across two cities. These datasets purport to cover the same spatial features, but our findings reveal wide discrepancies in accessibility results, driven by differences in dataset completeness, coverage, and accuracy between the sources. We provide guidelines for selecting and carefully validating data for accessibility analyses, as these decisions directly impact the accuracy and equity of downstream urban park planning and decision-making.

title: A utility-based framework for measuring perceived job accessibility using destination-mode choice models
authors: Matheus Fontenelle Siqueira, Carlos Felipe Grangeiro Loureiro
abstract: Perceived accessibility has become a central concept in accessibility research, but it is usually measured with psychometric scales, which are not decomposed into the components of accessibility, cannot be recomputed for new scenarios and carry no welfare interpretation. This paper argues that perceived accessibility can be measured with the expected maximum utility (logsum) of a discrete choice model whose choice set represents the alternatives the individual can use and knows, and whose valuations and perception of opportunities are estimated from behavior rather than imposed. The argument is developed from the mechanisms through which calculated and perceived accessibility diverge and applied to home-to-work travel of low-income workers in Fortaleza, Brazil, with a stated and revealed preference survey collected in 2024. The experiment screened the modes presented to each respondent by resources, distance and habitual use, so that the choice set reflects individual availability and awareness. Within a hierarchical structure, a mixed logit mode choice model estimated jointly on stated and revealed choices supplies a mode logsum for every zone, and a destination choice model with a random parameter estimates how the formal job mass is perceived. The measure contains the gravity measure as a restricted case, but estimates the trade-off between attractiveness and impedance, represents heterogeneous perceptions and multimodal availability, and carries a welfare interpretation. Valuations of time differ little between four gender and income strata, whereas the perception of job opportunities is strongly heterogeneous within each stratum. The resulting measure is individual, evaluative, awareness-conditioned and suitable for appraisal.

title: Preregistration as Cheap Talk: The Logic and Limits of Self-Enforcing Plans in Scientific Research
authors: Zion Little, Jacob Montgomery, Keith Schnakenberg
abstract: Preregistration has become increasingly prominent across scientific disciplines, with proponents claiming it reduces selective reporting and improves research credibility. Yet its logic is puzzling. Researchers face no formal penalty for straying from their stated plans; indeed, deviations are explicitly condoned. Why should simply announcing a plan change behavior? We address this question by modeling preregistration as a form of cheap talk in a model of private experimentation --- a costless, non-binding announcement that nonetheless shapes reviewer expectations and creates informal discipline through rational belief updating. We show that preregistration can be self-enforcing without any third-party oversight since deviations from an announced plan signal that undisclosed tests failed, and reviewers discount results accordingly. Scientists in our model thus voluntarily choose constraining plans since they lower the evidentiary bar for publication. But the very logic that explains the success of preregistration for enhancing researcher credibility makes its downstream consequences ambiguous. The plans scientists optimally choose retain substantial flexibility for selective reporting while still preserving the credibility benefits of preregistration. The result is that preregistration --- when researchers control plan design --- can produce higher false positive rates than an unrestrictive plan. We discuss how better institutional designs --- such as encouraging disclosure of all preregistered results, and ensuring plans are specific enough that such a norm is meaningful --- would more reliably achieve preregistration's intended goals.

title: Feminist Communication on Facebook: Rights Advocacy and Accompaniment. Text Mining of the Surkuna Case
authors: Jackeline Mendoza, Oscar Molina-Bailon, Yuly Marcillo
abstract: This study examined how feminist communication on Facebook connects rights violations, rights, and responses, drawing on 106 posts published in 2025 by Surkuna, an Ecuadorian organization. The analysis combined text mining, co-occurrence networks, and AI-assisted contextual coding. Messages regarding abortion linked autonomy to both overcoming access barriers and rejecting the forced imposition of the practice. Mobilization, consultation, or outreach appeared in 69% of posts containing institutional or regulatory demands, compared to 26% of all other messages. Accompaniment was expressed through offers of advisory services and accounts of support provided. In the case studied, rights advocacy gains meaning by connecting who can decide, who must respond, and what support is offered when violations occur. Ultimately, the findings provide empirical evidence on how autonomy, institutional accountability, and care are articulated within feminist communication.

title: Fundamental Causes of Crime at Places: Assessing Associations Among Neighborhood Types and Crime Rates Using Geodemographics
abstract: The paper discusses the role of contextual approaches in current spatial criminology, with its focus on variables, net-of-effects, and mechanism-identification. The study outlines how contextual approaches to understanding communities, such as geodemographics, have an affinity to modeling multiple, intertwined neighborhood dimensions. Using a specific-purpose geodemographic classification at the block-group level across Delaware (United States) and eight years of incident and arrest data (2010-2017), the paper shows how multidimensional neighborhood classifications are associated with multiple crime outcomes. The study thus shows how an in-depth descriptive approach can provide complementary insights to variable-centered practices in assessing neighborhood effects. Overall, the study highlights the need to consider fundamental causes in addition to proximal causes and echoes calls for upstream interventions to improve public security.

title: Restraint, Combat Roles, and Human-Rights Abuse: Cross-National Evidence on Policing and Militarisation
abstract: This article examines how restraint-oriented and militarised forms of policing relate to human-rights protection. It asks whether the organisational dynamics associated with police violence vary across these two policing models, and whether militarised practices erode restraint-oriented policing from within the same domestic-security system. I argue that militarisation, understood as involving both material coercive capacity and operational transformations through which military logics are introduced into domestic policing, may affect human-rights outcomes by intensifying the conditions associated with police use of force. Empirically, the article combines original cross-national indicators of policing practices in contentious politics with established measures of extrajudicial killings and physical-integrity violations. The analysis uses a global country-year panel covering 2010–2022, with operational policing models restricted to 2017–2022 due to ACLED coverage. The results show that restraint in contentious policing is associated with lower levels of extrajudicial killings and physical-integrity violations, while different forms of militarised policing are associated with higher levels of abuse. The conditional results further show that combat-oriented policing weakens the protective association between restrain policing and physical-integrity outcomes.The article contributes to the literature by distinguishing restraint-oriented policing, material militarisation, and operational police roles as separate dimensions of domestic coercive organisation. In doing so, it challenges the view of restraint and militarisation as simple opposites, showing instead that they may coexist and interact within the same domestic-security system.

title: Biased Provision: Cross-Provider Divergence in How LLMs and Search Engines Supply Evidence on Contested Political Questions
authors: Morgan Wack, Eva-Maria Vogel, Christian Pipal
abstract: Does the evidence generated to answer political questions depend on which large language model (LLM) users query? We introduce "biased provision" to describe this dependence, which can arise where providers differ in how compliant their models are to user requests. Auditing four LLMs, four search engines, and two hybrids across 8,249 responses to 30 claims, we find similar average rates of disconfirming evidence, evidence against the claim asked about, across system types but larger differences among LLMs. All four LLMs answered neutral questions with similar evidence but diverged once users asked for support, whereas search engines narrowed together only after queries included the user's argument. Search engines supplied the least disconfirming evidence under argued requests, a baseline for claims of chatbot sycophancy. As political questions migrate from search engines to chatbots, the evidence users receive will depend less on the tools people use than on which chatbot's answers they prefer.

title: Affective polarisation in CSES Module 6: a replication pipeline and an exploratory test of GenAI occupational exposure
abstract: This note makes the Reiljan Affective Polarization Index (API) available for CSES Module 6 elections and documents the pipeline that produces it. To our knowledge, as of October 2026, no published work reports API values from Module 6. We replicate published API scores to within 0.000002 (about six significant figures) for 12 elections (2007–2017) in ten countries that are covered by Reiljan et al.’s replication data, compute the index for eight Module 6 elections (five with usable occupation codes) held in 2022–24, and link party-level populism codes from PopuList 4.0 through Party Facts and ParlGov identifiers. As a demonstration, we test whether voters in occupations more exposed to generative AI are more or less affectively polarised, using five studies. Exposure is negatively associated with individual-level API (−0.135 per SD, p = .003), but the estimate falls to −0.082 (p = .27) with ISCO major-group fixed effects. The association with voting for populist parties behaves similarly (−3.1 pp, p = .004; −1.4 pp, p = .31 with ISCO major-group fixed effects). The exposure × populist interaction is not distinguishable from zero (p = .13). Only the far-right vote estimate stays below p = .05 with fixed effects, and it does not in the extended sample. We treat these results as a transparent null from an exploratory design, not as evidence of a causal mechanism. Code and aggregate scores are deposited on Zenodo.

title: Artificial intelligence and organizational change: a bibliometric mapping of AI as a tool and as an object of change (2000–2026)
authors: Angelo Leogrande, Mauro Di Molfetta, Valeria Nortarnicola, Maria Giovanna Trotta, Antonio Volpe Plantamura, Gianluca Zaza
abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) and organizational change is growing fast but fragmented. Two perspectives coexist: one uses AI, defined here as machine learning, natural language processing, generative AI and related intelligent systems, as a tool to diagnose, design, implement and monitor change; the other studies AI as the object whose adoption triggers change. We map the field and how the two perspectives relate. Of 1,402 Scopus records, a large language model applying a criterion calibrated on the author's judgment retained 525 documents (2000–2026). We combined performance analysis, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, keyword and topic analysis, and a coding of change phases. The field has grown by almost 70% a year since 2018, mostly through research on AI as an object; the share of studies using AI as a tool fell from 28% up to 2020 to 11% in 2024–2026. The two perspectives rest on largely separate references. Research on AI as an object forms eight research fronts; research on AI as a tool forms none, and almost half of its documents are disconnected from the main coupling network. Only 32 documents propose or evaluate AI as an instrument for managing change. Diagnosis dominates and studies that use AI across several phases of change are rare. These findings hold under alternative inclusion criteria, except the absence of a tool-based front, which reflects the narrow definition of AI adopted. We argue that the field lacks integration and validation rather than new algorithms, and propose an integrative framework with six propositions.

title: From Private Troubles to Public Issues: E-bike Mobility and Shared Space in Shenzhen
authors: YUMING ZHANG, Zehang Yu, YIXIN HUANG
abstract: When does e-bike mobility become a public issue concerning shared urban space? Drawing on the new mobilities paradigm and socio-technical regime theory, we develop the concept of "spatial publicness of mobility practices" through a case-based approach to complexity. We analyse 405 RedNote threads centred on Shenzhen, each comprising an original post, its static images and comments, using two-step qualitative comparative analysis. Socio-technical grounding in the original post, through technical mediation, spatial anchoring, public issue framing or practitioner positioning, is necessary for spatial publicness. Four sufficient configurations show how this grounding combines with situated articulation: a street setting shown without comment, a station entrance framed as a matter of public order, the work of keeping an owned vehicle usable, and commenters' standpoints on rules and enforcement. Much of what becomes public concerns vehicles at rest. The pavement becomes a borrowed mooring for e-bikes through repeated occupation, and its use becomes speakable mainly when something breaks. Where vehicles are privately owned, riders carry the work of joining rules made separately for sale, registration and road use, while the costs of enforcement fall unevenly across the city's labour and housing geography. Social media takes part in this system, making the occupation look ordinary and pooling the practical knowledge needed to settle notices and recover towed vehicles. The study offers a configurational and multimodal reading of how the use of shared space and its public interpretation become interconnected.

title: Equal on Facebook? Engagement and Vote Shares of European Parties, 2010 to 2020
abstract: Does social media level the field between large and small parties, or do the parties that win votes also win attention online? Research on this question, framed as equalisation against normalisation, has mostly studied what parties do online rather than how audiences respond. I compare each party's share of the interactions received by its country's party pages on Facebook with its share of the vote at the last national election, for 107 party pages in 16 European countries from 2010 to 2020 (875 party-years, 431 million interactions, collected through CrowdTangle). Engagement followed votes, but less than proportionally: a party with twice the vote share of another received about 1.7 times the engagement share (elasticity 0.79, SE 0.08), and 0.84 in the year after an election, when vote shares are freshest. This came almost entirely from what each post received rather than from how much parties posted, since small parties posted nearly as much as large ones. Parties with more than a fifth of the vote received a median of about 40% less of the engagement than of the vote, while at the median those with less than a tenth received slightly more. Engagement was about as concentrated across parties as the vote, but on different parties: the largest party by votes received the most engagement in only a quarter of country-years, well below what random variation around a proportional relationship would produce. Populist parties drew more than their vote share and governing parties less. These patterns did not change detectably over the decade. On Facebook, the attention of party audiences was neither simply normalised nor equalised: it was reordered, with the largest parties rarely at the top.

title: 超越“话语悬浮”：中西古今之争的结构性张力与文化主体性的实践重构
abstract: 摘 要：近年来，“中西古今之争”再度成为学界关注的焦点。然而，当前相关论述多陷于宏大叙事的“话语悬浮”，呈现出“高高举起，轻轻放下”的实践困境。本文认为，文化主体性的建构并非单纯的观念辩论或真理竞争，而是一个深刻的制度性实践过程。本文提出一个包含“话语资源供给”“意义框架建构”与“结构性负载传导”的三维分析模型。研究指出，当前宏大叙事之所以难以落地，微观机制在于个体的“认知带宽”被高强度的生存负载所挤占，导致反思性实践停滞；宏观机制在于新旧意义框架的更替未能跨越既有制度惯性的“路径依赖阈值”。破解这一百年难题，必须超越单纯的文本说服，转向三维同步的制度性干预：优先释放结构性负载以重塑反思空间，重构本土化的评价与分类体系，并通过高频、沉浸式的替代性文化实践完成意义系统的实质性累积。 关键词：中西古今之争；文化主体性；认知带宽；制度供给；路径依赖 Beyond "Discursive Suspension": Structural Tensions in the Debate on Chinese-Western and Ancient-Modern Relations and the Practical Reconstruction of Cultural Subjectivity Abstract: In recent years, the debate on "Chinese-Western and Ancient-Modern relations" has regained prominence in academic circles. However, current discourses often fall into "discursive suspension," presenting a practical dilemma of being "raised high but dropped lightly." This paper argues that the construction of cultural subjectivity is not merely a conceptual debate or a competition of truths, but a profound process of institutional practice. We propose a three-dimensional analytical model encompassing "discursive resource supply," "meaning framework construction," and "structural load transmission." The study indicates that the failure of grand narratives to take root is micro-mechanistically due to individuals' "cognitive bandwidth" being squeezed by high-intensity survival loads, leading to a stagnation of reflective practice. Macro-mechanistically, it is because the replacement of old and new meaning frameworks fails to cross the "path dependence threshold" of institutional inertia. To resolve this century-old dilemma, we must transcend mere textual persuasion and shift to three-dimensional, synchronized institutional interventions: prioritizing the release of structural loads to reshape reflective spaces, reconstructing localized evaluation and classification systems, and achieving substantial accumulation of meaning systems through high-frequency, immersive alternative cultural practices. Keywords: Chinese-Western and Ancient-Modern Debate; Cultural Subjectivity; Cognitive Bandwidth; Institutional Supply; Path Dependence

title: A Study of Control on Internal Monologue from Cognitive Neuroscience and Talk Therapy Perspective
abstract: This study investigated the relationship between self-talk, bilingualism, and cognitive control in a task-switching paradigm. Forty-five participants (34 bilingual, 11 monolingual) completed the Self-Talk Scale and a categorization task measuring mixing costs under auditory and visual cue conditions. We conducted independent samples t-tests and mixed-design ANOVAs to assess group differences. Monolingual participants reported significantly higher self-talk in self-reinforcement, self management, and social assessment, while no group differences were observed for self-criticism.
